newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Ex-Klansman Duke praises Australia's Hanson.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Klansman Duke praises Australia's Hanson.

text.p: Former Ku Klux Klan chief David Duke has backed Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson, handing ammunition to opponents out to demonstrate links between her and right-wing groups abroad.
A Melbourne newspaper on Friday quoted Duke, a leading U.S. rightwinger, as saying Hanson was as a true patriot protecting her country against outsiders.
Duke, a former Louisiana-based "Imperial Wizard" of the white supremacist Klan, told the Herald Sun he was aware of Hanson's views and admired her stand against multiculturalism.
"She is an Australian patriot," he told the daily.
"It is the prime minister (John Howard) who is out of line with traditional values. The prime minister is trying to destroy Australia's cultural and ethnic foundation.
"He doesn't care if Australia becomes a country where traditional Australians are a minority in their own country."
The Australian government, concerned that Hanson is damaging the nation's image among its biggest trading partners in Asia, pounced on the report, calling it an ugly development.

"It's a very ugly development and one which is good to see, in the sense that it's now exposing some of the cross links with the Hanson agenda," Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said after gleefully waving a copy of the front-page story, headlined "Klan Backs Hanson", at an Asian business breakfast.
"People will now be putting the microscope on all aspects of the Hanson agenda....Australia could well do without Ku Klux Klan endorsements or activities," Fischer told reporters.
Hanson says Australia is in danger of being swamped by Asians and her newly-created far-right One Nation party has drawn around 10 percent support in opinion polls.
Hanson told the Herald Sun she had no contact with Duke and was shocked by his endorsement.
"I have maintained my independence. I will not be associated with extremists," she said.

But influential government figure Ron Boswell and former foreign minister Gareth Evans, now deputy leader of the Labor opposition, said the former fish-and-chip shop owner had ties with Australian groups urging violent and racist policies.
"There is no doubt that she is linked with the militant crazy right and they with her," Evans said on Thursday.
Boswell told the Senate Hanson's One Nation was linked to the far-right League of Rights, militant gun lobby groups and other extremist factions.
Howard labels Hanson an extremist but still faces criticism for failing to react firmly enough when Hanson first sparked a divisive race row a year ago.
Howard's current visit to Britain has fallen under Hanson's shadow, with the issue of race relations in Australia emerging as a prominent theme of newspaper coverage of his trip.
